newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany considering petrol tax rise to plug gap.
newsitem.headline: Germany considering petrol tax rise to plug gap.

text.p: Germany's centre-right coalition government met on Wednesday to discuss a petrol tax hike to plug a financing hole created by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) rejecting key parts of its 1997 tax bill.

But coalition sources said a decision would have to wait until the SPD, which holds the majority in the upper house of parliament, comes up with ways to cover a revenue shortfall caused by the scrapping of a wealth tax and rise in child benefits.
"This is a subject we must discuss," Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt of the Free Democrats (FDP) coalition party told reporters.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel has said the multi-billion mark shortfall next year would not threaten Germany's ability to qualify for the launch of the single European currency in 1999.
Germany will overshoot Maastricht's budget deficit ceiling of three percent of GDP this year, but Waigel stuck to his 2.5 percent target next year despite the tax bill setback.
Politicians were reluctant to commit publicly to a petrol tax hike which opposition SPD members said could cost German motorists as much as seven billion marks ($4.54 billion).

The tax bill was part of a 70 billion mark austerity plan intended to reduce the tax burden and stimulate job creation in Germany, suffering from unemployment stuck near four million despite an accelerating economic recovery.
But it always ran the risk of being wrecked by the SPD, which controls the Bundesrat upper house of parliament, giving it the power to block tax plans.
The stalemate means the wealth tax, ruled unconstitutional by a court, will be abolished from the start of 1997 -- hitting regional governments with a revenue loss of nine billion marks.
The SPD block also means a 20 mark increase in monthly child benefits to 220 marks will go ahead automatically -- at a cost of 5.5 billion marks. Waigel had wanted to defer the rise.
The losses will be offset partly by changes in inheritance tax and other revisions which should still become law. But that still leaves a hefty revenue gap.
The Munich Abendzeitung newspaper said earlier that Waigel's Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) was mulling a petrol tax hike of 10-15 pfennigs a litre.

Drivers now pay around 1.55 marks for a litre of unleaded petrol, of which 98 pfennigs is tax. Petrol taxes raise 65 billion marks a year, and each one-pfennig increase would bring a further 700 million marks into state coffers, experts say.
SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss said a petrol tax hike could be squeezed in later on -- even though talks on the tax bill should have been wound up this week.

But he remained critical. "The whole thing is completely stupid. We are not talking about practical policy -- only about plugging holes in the budget," he told the B.Z. newspaper in an article to be published on Thursday.
Other leaders of the FDP said they wanted to stick to a pact with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) that any tax increases would have to be offset by reductions.

The tax deadlock also means that Waigel will not be able to abolish a capital trading tax, seen by businesses as hindering enterprise and investment. It will now have to be imposed in depressed eastern Germany.
The tax juggling could not come at a worse time for Germany as it seeks to consolidate itself as the stable cornerstone of Europe's project for economic and monetary union (EMU).
Kohl met Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar on Tuesday to discuss Madrid's chances of qualifying for EMU, and has invited Italian premier Romano Prodi to dinner on Thursday. ($1=1.5405 Mark)
